guideTitle: Best Solar Generators for Your House (2026)
metaTitle: Best Solar Generators for Your House (2026)
metaDescription: Five solar generators for house outages, from a 1,024Wh essentials unit to a 5,040Wh split-phase battery, with honest load math for real homes.
expertTake: The Jackery Solar Generator 5000 Plus is the best house pick because its 7,200W, 120/240V output can actually feed a home panel through a transfer switch. The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic is the value pick for people who only need the refrigerator, router and a few lights. Skip all of these if you want to run central air or an electric range, because that takes a permanently installed home battery.
introParagraphs: Powering a house from a portable battery is a question of priorities. Nobody expects a plug-in unit to run every circuit, so the real work is deciding which handful of loads matter during an outage and sizing a machine that carries them without drama.

We looked at five solar generators that make sense for a home, from a compact essentials unit up to a large split-phase battery. Each is judged on usable energy, how it connects to household wiring, and how well it handles recharging from panels during a multi-day outage.

products.name: Jackery Solar Generator 5000 Plus with 2x200W Panels
products.description:
Large home appliances are what this machine is built for. At 7,200W rated with a 14,400W surge and support for both 120V and 240V, it can run a well pump, a refrigerator, a gas furnace blower and a window air conditioner at once, and it can feed a home through a transfer switch the way a generator would. The 5,040Wh tank is large enough that a typical essentials load of 1.5 to 2kW lasts a long evening.

Its big advantage over a gas generator is silence and zero fuel logistics, and the listing says it expands to 60kWh with extra batteries and accepts both high and low voltage panels. The weak point is the standard 400W of panels: refilling 5,040Wh from 400W of real-world panel output takes several days, so you plan to charge from the grid between outages or add a bigger array.

Store it in a dry indoor spot such as a garage or basement, check the vent screens each season, and keep it around half charged if it will sit for months. Test the transfer switch under load once a year so you know it works before the storm arrives.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who want a battery that can feed a panel for a multi-day outage.
pros: Accepts both high and low voltage panels
cons: Needs a proper transfer switch install

products.name: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3,600Wh Power Station, 120V 3,600W
products.description:
The DELTA Pro has been a home-backup staple for years, and that history shows in the ecosystem around it. A 3,600Wh LFP battery with 3,600W of output, expandable to 4,500W with an accessory, runs a refrigerator, a freezer, internet gear, lights and a microwave together. Recharge is the other story: the listing quotes about 1.8 hours from a 240V outlet and 2.7 hours from a standard circuit.

That quick recharge matters in a multi-day outage because you can charge fast when grid power flickers back, then run on battery again. Compared with the Jackery 5000 Plus it carries about 1,440Wh less energy and produces half the output, but it is a lot easier to move and has a wider range of accessories and third-party transfer-kit support.

Keep it somewhere dry and cool, vacuum the fan inlets once a season and run it under a moderate load every few months. A watt meter on each appliance tells you which circuits can share the battery.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who want a mature platform with fast recharge and broad accessory support.
pros: Quick charging from 240V in under two hours
LFP cells rated for long cycle life
cons: Listed as 120V, so one leg of a home panel
Older design than the newest rivals

products.name: OSCAL PowerMax 6000 with 3x400W Solar Panels
products.description:
The PowerMax 6000 appeals to anyone who needs 240V for a well pump or a clothes dryer but cannot justify the largest battery on the market. It delivers 6,000W split-phase from a 3,600Wh tank, so you can start big motors but must budget energy carefully, because those loads drain a 3.6kWh pack in an hour or two.

Its best feature is solar: 2,400W of input and three 400W panels in the kit mean a sunny day can nearly refill the tank, something the Jackery 5000 Plus cannot do with its 400W kit. For a home with a ground-mount array spot, that closes the loop in a multi-day outage.

The panels are big, so plan where they will sit and how to anchor them in wind. Check connectors each season and keep the unit indoors, away from damp walls.
products.bestFor: Homes that need 240V now and want a large included solar array to refill it.
pros: 2,400W solar input refills in a day
cons: Large panels need real yard space

products.name: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 with 2x200W Solar Panels
products.description:
This is the sensible middle of the lineup. 2,080Wh and 2,600W of output run a refrigerator, a chest freezer, a router and a sump pump together, and the listing notes standby consumption of about 10W, so it does not bleed charge while it waits. The kit includes two 200W panels and lists a full solar recharge in about five and a half hours of good sun.

Compared with the DELTA Pro it holds 1,520Wh less energy but is far lighter and less awkward in a hall closet. Against the DELTA 3 Classic it has twice the capacity and 800W more output at a moderate premium. It fills the sweet spot for a household whose critical loads add up to about 600W continuous.

The cells use an automotive-grade LiFePO4 chemistry with a claimed long life. Keep it indoors, run a quick discharge test each season and cycle the battery from 20 percent to 90 percent now and then to keep the monitoring accurate.
products.bestFor: Homes whose essentials draw under 800W and who want solar included.
pros: Two 200W panels refill in a day
Lighter and easier to place than 3kWh units
cons: 2,080Wh runs out quickly under heavy load
No transfer switch listed in the kit

products.name: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic 1,024Wh, 1,800W AC
products.description:
For a household that only wants the refrigerator, router, phones and a lamp alive during an outage, this small, fast-charging unit is enough. 1,024Wh with 1,800W of output keeps a typical refrigerator running for about a day. The listing claims a 10ms UPS switchover, so a modem and desktop PC will not drop when the grid fails.

Its strength is recharge speed, about 45 minutes to 80 percent from the wall, which means short grid windows do real work. It lacks the capacity for pumps or air conditioners, and it does not have the DELTA Pro's expansion path, so treat it as a first step.

It weighs a fraction of the big units, so it lives in a closet and moves with you. A watt meter on the refrigerator tells you its true consumption, and storing the unit half charged keeps the battery healthy.
products.bestFor: Renters and apartment owners who want a fast-charging essentials battery.
pros: Fast zero to 80 percent in 45 minutes
10ms UPS keeps routers and PCs running
cons: 1,024Wh covers about one day of a refrigerator
Cannot run well pumps or central air

products.name: ABOK Ark3600 3,840Wh with 500W Alternator Charger
products.description:
Fifteen output ports and a 3,840Wh tank make the Ark3600 a household hub rather than a single-purpose box. The listing says the 3,600W inverter supports almost all household appliances, and extra batteries lift capacity to 11,520Wh, so you can buy one now and add storage later without replacing the inverter.

The odd extra in this listing is a 500W alternator charger, which matters at home only if you have a vehicle to idle in a prolonged outage: a truck or car can top the battery up when the sun is absent. Against the DELTA Pro it holds 240Wh more energy and has a similar 3,600W output, though it is a newer platform with fewer third-party transfer kits.

Plan where the expansion packs will sit before you buy, since stacking heavy batteries on a garage shelf is a safety issue. Keep the vents clear, and run it under load a few times a year so the battery management system stays calibrated.
products.bestFor: Households that want to start with one battery and add storage over time.
pros: 15 output ports run many small devices
500W alternator charger as a backup refill
3,600W rated output at a moderate size
cons: No solar panels in this bundle
Newer platform with fewer transfer-kit options

buyingCriteria.explanation: A refrigerator uses 100 to 200W running but 3 times that at startup, a sump pump 800 to 1,200W, and a furnace blower around 500W. Add them up before you pick a machine. The DELTA 3 Classic's 1,800W covers a refrigerator, router and lights, while the Jackery 5000 Plus's 7,200W also covers a well pump.

A 600W average load drains the Elite 200 V2's 2,080Wh in roughly three hours, but the Jackery 5000 Plus lasts closer to seven. Multiply your average draw by the hours you want to ride through, then divide by 0.85 for inverter losses.

Well pumps, dryers and ranges often need 240V. The Oscal PowerMax 6000 and the Jackery 5000 Plus offer it, while the DELTA Pro, Elite 200 V2 and DELTA 3 Classic are 120V. Do not buy a 120V unit for a 240V pump.

Plugging appliances into extension cords works for essentials, but backfeeding a home panel needs a transfer switch or interlock installed by an electrician. Skipping it is a real safety risk for utility workers and for your house wiring. Budget for installation.

The Oscal accepts 2,400W of solar and ships with 1,200W of panels, while the Jackery 5000 Plus ships with 400W. Real panel output is 60 to 80 percent of label. A larger array turns a multi-day outage from a countdown into a routine.

An inverter that stays on burns power with no load; the Elite 200 V2 lists about 10W standby. A claimed 10ms UPS function keeps computers on, but it only matters if you leave the unit plugged in and charged.

howWeEvaluated.title: Home-backup suitability
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged whether each machine can sensibly serve a house: output, voltage and how it connects. The Jackery 5000 Plus and Oscal PowerMax 6000 earned the highest marks for 240V support. 120V-only units were scored for essentials use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Runtime for real loads
howWeEvaluated.description: We modeled a refrigerator, router and lights at about 300W average. The DELTA 3 Classic's 1,024Wh covers that for about three hours of full load, while the Jackery 5000 Plus runs it for over 14.

howWeEvaluated.title: Recharge in an outage
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared solar input limits and included panels. The Oscal's 2,400W input and 1,200W of panels beat the 400W kits of the Jackery and Bluetti.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety and install path
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for transfer-switch support and safe connection routes, since backfeeding a panel improperly is dangerous. The Jackery and EcoFlow ecosystems offer clearer paths than the newer brands.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership and weight
howWeEvaluated.description: We used the spec sheets and owner feedback patterns to rate how awkward each unit is to live with. The DELTA 3 Classic is easy to move, while the Jackery 5000 Plus needs a permanent spot.

rows: Multiple fast recharges from the wall

cards.label: Plug-in appliances
cards.text: Run extension cords to the refrigerator and a few outlets. The DELTA 3 Classic and Elite 200 V2 are built for this and need no electrician. It is cheap and flexible, but you manage cords.

cards.label: Transfer switch
cards.text: A switch lets the Jackery 5000 Plus or Oscal PowerMax 6000 feed chosen circuits through the panel. It is the right way to run a furnace blower or a well pump.

howToChoose.note: Choose plug-in for refrigerator-only needs, transfer switch when hardwired loads matter.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for 240V output and a surge rating at least three times the pump's running watts. A half-horsepower pump runs around 1,000W and starts near 3,000W.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Oscal PowerMax 6000 and the Jackery 5000 Plus are the only two with 240V. The Jackery's 14,400W surge gives the most headroom.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your home has a well, a furnace blower or medical equipment. Step up to the Jackery 5000 Plus or the Oscal PowerMax 6000 for the 240V and the bigger tank.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only need a refrigerator and communication gear. The DELTA 3 Classic or the Elite 200 V2 does that.

maintenance.why: Running a real load confirms the inverter and cells still perform. It also catches a fault before the storm does.

maintenance.task: Test the transfer switch or interlock
maintenance.why: Switch contacts can stick or corrode. A test under load confirms safe operation.
Moderate charge lengthens LiFePO4 life. Top up every few months.
Dust reduces airflow and limits full-load runtime.
Corroded or loose connectors lose power and heat up.

faq.q: Can a solar generator power a whole house?
faq.a: Not in the way a standby generator can. The Jackery 5000 Plus can feed chosen circuits for days, but central air and electric ranges would drain it in hours. Plan around essentials.

faq.q: Do I need a transfer switch?
faq.a: If you want circuits like a furnace blower or a well pump on battery, yes, installed by an electrician. For a refrigerator and lights, extension cords work.

faq.q: Which is the best value for a house?
faq.a: The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic is the lowest cost for a refrigerator and router, and the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 adds capacity and panels for a moderate step up. Both are sensible first buys.

faq.q: Is peak power the figure that matters?
faq.a: No. Rated watts decide what runs together, and surge only covers a fraction of a second. The Jackery 5000 Plus's 14,400W surge is useful headroom, but 7,200W is its real limit.

faq.q: How do I recharge in a long outage?
faq.a: Use solar, and a larger array helps. The Oscal's 1,200W kit refills far faster than the 400W kits. Between storms, recharge from the grid when it returns.
LiFePO4 stations produce no exhaust and run indoors, unlike gas generators. Give them airflow and keep them away from water and heat.
